Birds that decide the trip

Puffins in England

The Farne Islands put you closer to breeding puffins than almost anywhere in Britain, because the birds nest beside the visitor paths and ignore you completely. Boats run from Seahouses and land on Inner Farne and Staple Island through the season.

When Late April to late July, with the birds gone by early August

Where Northumberland and the Farne Islands, The Yorkshire coast: Bempton and Spurn

Gannets in England

Bempton Cliffs is the only mainland gannetry in England, and the birds pass the clifftop viewpoints at eye level all day. It is the easiest seabird colony in the country to reach: a car park, a path and a set of railed platforms.

When March to October, at its fullest from May to July

Where The Yorkshire coast: Bempton and Spurn

Bitterns in England

English bitterns came within a handful of booming males in the 1990s and have recovered on reedbeds created for them. The Norfolk Broads, the Somerset Levels and the Suffolk coast hold most of them, and booming carries a long way over flat ground on a still morning.

When February to May for booming; winter for birds feeding in the open

Where The Norfolk coast and the Broads, The Somerset Levels and the Severn, Suffolk and the Essex coast

Cranes in England

Cranes returned to Norfolk on their own in 1979 and were reintroduced to the Somerset Levels from 2010. Both populations breed now, and the Somerset Levels flock is the easier of the two to find, usually on the wet grassland around Ham Wall and Greylake.

When All year; easiest in winter when the birds flock

Where The Somerset Levels and the Severn, The Norfolk coast and the Broads

Red Kites in England

The Chilterns reintroduction that began in 1989 is one of the most visible conservation successes in Britain. Kites are now unmissable over the M40 corridor and have spread across southern and central England from there.

When All year

Where The Chilterns, the Thames and the London reservoirs

Black-tailed Godwits in England

The Wash and the Ribble take godwits in tens of thousands on passage and through the winter, and the Ouse and Nene Washes hold the small breeding population that has been nursed back from almost nothing.

When Passage in spring and autumn, biggest counts October to March

Where The Wash and the Lincolnshire coast, Morecambe Bay and the Cumbrian coast

Dartford Warblers in England

A resident warbler on lowland heath, and one that a hard winter can still knock back badly. The New Forest and the Dorset heaths hold the strongest populations, and the birds sing from gorse tops on a calm morning.

When All year; easiest March to June when singing

Where The New Forest, Dorset and Poole Harbour, Kent, Sussex and the south coast

Spoonbills in England

Spoonbills began breeding again in England in 2010 after an absence of three centuries, and Holkham in north Norfolk now holds the largest colony. Birds feed on the shallow pools and creeks along the same coast.

When March to September

Where The Norfolk coast and the Broads, Suffolk and the Essex coast

When to Go

The English birding year has three peaks rather than one. Seabirds fill the cliffs from March to July, migration runs along the coasts through August to October, and the estuaries hold their biggest flocks from November to February.

Spring

March to June

Seabirds come back to the ledges in March, summer migrants arrive through April, and by May every woodland is singing from before five in the morning.

Go for Breeding seabirds, full song, and the longest days of the year in the north.

Trade off Rooms cost the most from Easter onward, and island boats need booking weeks ahead in June.

Typical daily average
  • March: 3 to 9 °C / 37 to 48 °F
  • April: 4 to 12 °C / 39 to 54 °F
  • May: 7 to 15 °C / 45 to 59 °F
  • June: 10 to 18 °C / 50 to 64 °F

Autumn

July to October

Wader passage builds from July, the coasts fill with migrants through September, and October is when a rarity can turn up almost anywhere.

Go for Big wader counts, seabirds moving past in an onshore wind, and the best chance of a bird from a long way off course.

Trade off Song has stopped, so birds are identified on plumage and call, and the seabird colonies are empty by August.

Typical daily average
  • July: 12 to 19 °C / 54 to 66 °F
  • August: 12 to 19 °C / 54 to 66 °F
  • September: 10 to 17 °C / 50 to 63 °F
  • October: 8 to 13 °C / 46 to 55 °F

Winter

November to February

Geese, swans and waders pack the estuaries, starlings gather over the reedbeds at dusk, and raptors are easy over open ground.

Go for Six figure goose and wader flocks, murmurations, and reserves you have largely to yourself.

Trade off Daylight is short, and the boats to the Farne Islands stop for the winter.

Typical daily average
  • November: 5 to 10 °C / 41 to 50 °F
  • December: 3 to 8 °C / 37 to 46 °F
  • January: 2 to 7 °C / 36 to 45 °F
  • February: 2 to 7 °C / 36 to 45 °F

RSPB Rainham Marshes is twenty minutes from Fenchurch Street by train and sits on the Thames wall. Half a day gets you marsh, reedbed and estuary and back to the airport.

The most concentrated run of reserves in England, all on one coast road. Time the last morning for a big tide at Snettisham, which is the finest wader spectacle in the country.

Three estuaries and a wetland centre in four days, all within an hour of one another. Work the Dee on a rising tide from Parkgate, then move north for the geese at Marshside and Martin Mere.

England End to End

Newcastle (NCL), Yorkshire, Lincolnshire, Norfolk, Suffolk, Kent, the New Forest, Somerset

The full sweep from north to south. It takes the seabird colonies first and finishes on the reedbeds and heaths, and May and June are best, when every breeder is nesting at once.

Northumberland and the Farne Islands

Basalt seabird islands and a tidal dune coast, ninety minutes north of Newcastle

A dune and castle coast with a cluster of low basalt islands lying offshore. Landing on Inner Farne in June puts you inside an Arctic tern colony that defends itself vigorously, and grey seals haul out on the rocks below.

  • Habitat: Whin sill cliff and low islands off a dune coast, with Lindisfarne's mudflats and saltmarsh behind and the Cheviot moorland inland.
  • When: May to July for the tern and puffin colonies on the islands. October to March for pale-bellied brent, grey plover and wigeon on the Lindisfarne flats.
  • Getting there: Boats to the Farnes run from Seahouses on the B1340. Lindisfarne is reached over a tidal causeway off the A1, and the crossing times are published and absolute.
  • Look for: Atlantic Puffin, Common Murre, Black-legged Kittiwake, Arctic Tern, Roseate Tern, Common Eider
  • Parks and reserves: Farne Islands (island reserve), Lindisfarne National Nature Reserve, Coquet Island (island reserve), Newton Pool (reserve)
  • Stops:
    • : A working harbour and the departure point for Farne Islands boat trips. National Trust landing tickets are sold from the quayside kiosk, and puffins and seals come close to the boats.
    • : A tidal bay inside the Lindisfarne National Nature Reserve, free from a roadside pull-in on the A1. Wigeon and pink-footed geese roost across the mudflats in winter.
    • : The tidal causeway linking Holy Island to the mainland. It can be crossed only within the published tide times, and waders and wildfowl feed on the flats it crosses.
    • : A working harbour on the Coquet estuary and the departure point for boat trips around Coquet Island, which is closed to landing. Roseate and Arctic terns fish offshore in summer.
    • : A clifftop and shore path along the Northumberland coast, free to walk between the fishing village of Craster and Dunstanburgh Castle. Eiders bob close inshore and skuas pass offshore.
    • Inner Farne landing trip : A boat trip with a possible landing on Inner Farne, booked through the National Trust kiosk at Seahouses. Arctic terns dive at your head and eiders sit on the path.
  • Visitor centres: National Trust Farne Islands landing point, Seahouses
  • Also covers: Alnwick, Amble Harbour, Bamburgh, Budle Bay, Coquet Island, Craster to Dunstanburgh Castle path, Holy Island Causeway, Inner Farne landing trip, Lindisfarne National Nature Reserve, National Trust Farne Islands landing point, Seahouses, Newton Pool, Seahouses Harbour
  • Also watch for: The Farne Islands hold one of England's largest grey seal colonies, with pups born on the rocks between October and December. Harbour porpoises and, in late summer, minke whales are seen from the boats, and Atlantic grey seals often surface right alongside them.

Morecambe Bay and the Cumbrian coast

Tidal saltmarsh, shingle spit and sandstone sea cliff around the shores of Cumbria

Two great tidal bays either side of the Cumbrian coast, with the largest reedbed in northwest England behind one of them. Morecambe Bay lifts wader flocks off the sand on a rising tide in numbers that are hard to take in.

  • Habitat: The largest continuous intertidal flat in Britain, with saltmarsh, raised mosses and the red sandstone seabird cliff at St Bees behind it.
  • When: October to March for the wader roosts at high tide, which is the whole point of the bay. May to July for the St Bees auks.
  • Getting there: The A590 and A5087 run the southern shore, and Leighton Moss has its own station on the Lancaster to Barrow line. St Bees is signed off the A595.
  • Look for: Eurasian Bittern, Bearded Reedling, Western Marsh Harrier, Red Knot, Barnacle Goose, Common Murre
  • Parks and reserves: Arnside and Silverdale National Landscape, Lake District National Park, Solway Coast National Landscape
  • Stops:
    • RSPB Leighton Moss : An RSPB reserve with a visitor centre and reedbed hides, open every day of the year with an entry fee for non-members. Bittern, marsh harrier and bearded reedling hold the reeds.
    • RSPB Hodbarrow : An RSPB reserve on a former iron ore works beside the Duddon estuary, walked from the car park at any time. Terns, eider and wintering wildfowl use the lagoon.
    • South Walney : A Cumbria Wildlife Trust reserve at the tip of Walney Island, a short walk from the car park with a small fee for non-members. Grey seals haul out on the shingle spit.
    • RSPB Campfield Marsh : An RSPB reserve on the Solway Firth saltmarsh, walked from the car park and hide, open every day without charge. Barnacle geese and golden plover winter on the merse.
    • : A stretch of the Morecambe Bay shoreline, from a roadside car park at the end of Hest Bank Lane. Waders and wildfowl gather here on the incoming tide.
    • RSPB Haweswater : An RSPB and United Utilities reserve above the reservoir in the Lake District, walked from the car park at Mardale Head. Ring ouzel and curlew breed on the fells above.
    • St Bees Head : An RSPB reserve on Cumbria's only stretch of cliff coastline, on a clifftop path from the car park in St Bees. Guillemots, razorbills and kittiwakes nest on the ledges.
    • Hest Bank at Morecambe Bay : An RSPB reserve with free access from the shore road and no visitor centre. Knot, dunlin and godwits swirl up off the sands in the hour before high tide.
  • Visitor centres: RSPB Leighton Moss Visitor Centre, South Walney Nature Reserve (Cumbria Wildlife Trust)
  • Also covers: Arnside and Silverdale National Landscape, Barrow-in-Furness, Carnforth, Grange-over-Sands, Hest Bank at Morecambe Bay, Keswick, Lake District National Park, RSPB Campfield Marsh, RSPB Haweswater, RSPB Hodbarrow, RSPB Leighton Moss Visitor Centre, Solway Coast National Landscape, South Walney Nature Reserve (Cumbria Wildlife Trust), St Bees Head
  • Also watch for: Grey seals haul out on the shingle at South Walney and pup there between October and December, while natterjack toads call from the dune slacks of the Solway coast on warm nights in May and June. Red squirrels still hold on in the oakwoods around Haweswater, one of Cumbria's last strongholds for the species.

The Dee, the Mersey and the Ribble

Estuary sand, grazed saltmarsh and dock lagoon between the Wirral and the Lancashire coast

Three estuaries lie within an hour of one another across the north-west, and each one fills with waders and wildfowl from October onwards. The Ribble carries more than a quarter of a million birds through the winter, which makes it the most important wildfowl estuary in Britain. Pink-footed geese move between its marshes and the flooded pastures at Martin Mere in flocks that peak around 34,000.

  • Habitat: Sand and mud flats with grazed saltmarsh behind them on the Dee and the Ribble, spoil lagoons beside the Manchester Ship Canal at Frodsham, and fixed dunes along the Sefton coast.
  • When: October to March for the geese, the swans and the high-tide wader roosts. September to November after two or three days of north-west gale for the seabirds off the Wirral.
  • Getting there: The M53 runs the length of the Wirral to the Dee shore and the M58 reaches the Lancashire mosses from Liverpool. Merseyrail serves Hoylake and West Kirby, and Southport, Burscough Bridge, Chester and Neston all have stations.
  • Look for: Pink-footed Goose, Whooper Swan, Northern Pintail, Black-tailed Godwit, Little Gull, Leach's Storm Petrel
  • Stops:
    • RSPB Burton Mere Wetlands : An RSPB reserve of pools and scrapes on the Cheshire shore of the Dee, walked from the car park with an entry fee for non-members. Wildfowl and waders use the scrapes all winter and avocets breed on them.
    • RSPB Parkgate : A viewpoint over the Dee saltmarsh from the old sea wall at Parkgate, free at any hour. The highest tides push water rails, short-eared owls and harriers off the marsh in front of the wall.
    • RSPB Marshside : An RSPB reserve of coastal grassland and pools on the edge of Southport, open daily, with a car park on Marine Drive. Pink-footed geese feed on the fields inland and lapwings and redshanks breed on the marsh.
    • RSPB Hesketh Out Marsh : An RSPB reserve of restored saltmarsh on the inner Ribble, with a viewing shelter over a tidal scrape and a car park off Dib Road. Wigeon, pintail and black-tailed godwits gather here through the winter.
    • WWT Martin Mere : A WWT centre of flooded pasture and pools in the south Lancashire mosses, open daily with an entry fee for non-members and twelve hides. Whooper swans and pink-footed geese roost here in thousands.
    • Seaforth Nature Reserve : A Lancashire Wildlife Trust reserve of two lagoons inside Liverpool docks, with access by arrangement with the trust. Spring brings the largest gathering of little gulls in Britain.
    • Lunt Meadows : A Lancashire Wildlife Trust reserve of wet grassland and reedbed on the Alt floodplain, walked from the car park at any time without charge. Marsh harriers quarter the reeds and snipe winter on the wet fields.
    • : A seafront and marine lake at the mouth of the Mersey, with shelters by the fort for watching the sea. North-west gales in autumn bring Leach's storm petrels past the point.
  • Visitor centres: WWT Martin Mere Wetland Centre, RSPB Burton Mere Wetlands visitor centre
  • Also covers: Burscough, Chester, Crosby, Frodsham, Hoylake, Liverpool, Lunt Meadows, Lytham St Annes, Neston, New Brighton, RSPB Burton Mere Wetlands visitor centre, RSPB Hesketh Out Marsh, RSPB Marshside, RSPB Parkgate, Seaforth Nature Reserve, Southport, West Kirby, WWT Martin Mere Wetland Centre
  • Also watch for: Red squirrels hold the birch and pine woodland at Freshfield Dune Heath behind the Sefton coast, and sand lizards bask on the open heath beside them. Water voles live in the Wham Dyke on the same reserve, and the dune slacks further along the coast carry great crested newts and the liverwort petalwort.

The Peak District and the Pennines

Moorland, dale and gritstone between Manchester, Sheffield and Leeds

Blanket bog, gritstone edge and limestone dale along the spine of England, within an hour of several large cities. This is where the breeding waders and the moorland birds are, and where the walking is the point.

  • Habitat: Blanket bog and heather moor on gritstone, with cloughs of oak and reservoirs in the valleys between.
  • When: April to July for breeding waders and ring ouzel on the edges. Winter brings the moorland raptors down to the reservoir margins.
  • Getting there: The A57 Snake Pass and A628 cross the moors from Manchester and Sheffield, both within an hour. The reservoirs have their own car parks off the valley roads.
  • Look for: Red Grouse, Eurasian Curlew, European Golden Plover, Ring Ouzel, Black Grouse, Merlin
  • Parks and reserves: Peak District National Park, Yorkshire Dales National Park, North Pennines National Landscape, Forest of Bowland National Landscape
  • Stops:
    • : An open gritstone moor above the Derwent reservoirs, walked from roadside car parks at any time. Ring ouzel, merlin and red grouse hold the heather and tors.
    • Eastern Moors (Big Moor and Curbar Gap) : A National Trust and RSPB partnership reserve on Sheffield's edge, walked from free car parks at Curbar Gap or Big Moor. Curlew and ring ouzel work the heather.
    • : A wooded reservoir valley in the Peak District, walked from the Errwood car park and open at any time. Ring ouzel and curlew hold the moor edges above the water.
    • Upper Teesdale : A National Nature Reserve in the North Pennines, from Bowlees Visitor Centre or across the Cow Green Reservoir causeway. Golden plover, curlew and black grouse use the limestone moor.
    • Malham Tarn : A National Nature Reserve and England's highest marl lake, from the National Trust car park in the Yorkshire Dales. Curlew and snipe breed on the fen around it.
    • Malham Cove, Yorkshire Dales : A limestone amphitheatre in the Yorkshire Dales, on foot from a free car park and open at any time. Peregrine falcons nest on the cliff face most summers.
    • Langden Brook, Forest of Bowland : A moorland valley in the Forest of Bowland, walked from a roadside car park in the Trough of Bowland. It is one of England's best places for breeding merlin.
  • Visitor centres: Bowlees Visitor Centre, Yorkshire Dales National Park Centre, Malham
  • Also covers: Bakewell, Bowlees Visitor Centre, Castleton, Derwent Edge, Eastern Moors (Big Moor and Curbar Gap), Forest of Bowland National Landscape, Hebden Bridge, Langden Brook, Forest of Bowland, Malham Cove, Yorkshire Dales, Malham Tarn, Middleton-in-Teesdale, North Pennines National Landscape, Peak District National Park, Settle, The Goyt Valley, Upper Teesdale, Yorkshire Dales National Park Centre, Malham
  • Also watch for: Mountain hares still wear white winter coats on the high moors above Derwent Edge from December to February, and red deer graze the bracken slopes of the Eastern Moors through autumn. Upper Teesdale's sugar limestone grassland flowers with spring gentian and globeflower in May and June, a rarity found almost nowhere else in England.

Spurn Bird Observatory

The Yorkshire coast: Bempton and Spurn

Two seabird and migration headlands an hour apart on the East Yorkshire coast

Chalk cliffs at one end and a shifting sand spit at the other, an hour apart. Bempton gives eye level views of England's only mainland gannet colony, and Spurn funnels migration into a strip of land a few hundred metres wide.

  • Habitat: Chalk cliff at Bempton and a shifting sand and shingle spit at Spurn, with the Humber mudflats on its inner side.
  • When: April to August for the Bempton gannets and auks. September to November at Spurn is one of the best migration watches in Britain, and an easterly is what makes it.
  • Getting there: Bempton Cliffs is signed off the B1229 with a station at Bempton on the Hull to Scarborough line. Spurn is reached on the B1445 through Kilnsea, and the point beyond is walked or taken by the reserve's own vehicle.
  • Look for: Northern Gannet, Black-legged Kittiwake, Atlantic Puffin, Common Murre, Razorbill, Little Tern
  • Parks and reserves:
    • RSPB Bempton Cliffs (RSPB reserve), An RSPB reserve with a visitor centre and a parking charge. Its clifftop platforms give eye level views onto the ledges of England's only mainland gannet colony, alongside kittiwakes, puffins and guillemots.
    • Flamborough Cliffs Nature Reserve
    • Spurn National Nature Reserve
    • Kilnsea Wetlands Nature Reserve
  • Stops:
    • Flamborough Head, South Landing : A Yorkshire Wildlife Trust reserve with a small seas centre and free access. A clifftop path leads out from the beach, and auks and gannets pass the headland on the way to Bempton.
    • Kilnsea Wetlands : A Yorkshire Wildlife Trust reserve with hides, free to visit from a roadside car park. Migrant waders and wildfowl use the freshwater scrapes behind the sea wall.
    • : A fenced lagoon on the beach between Kilnsea and Easington, with free access from the path. Yorkshire's only little tern colony nests here and is wardened through the summer.
    • Spurn Point : The tip of a narrow shifting sand spit within the National Nature Reserve, free to visit on foot along the sea defence. Migrating seabirds pass close by the point in autumn winds.
  • Visitor centres:
    • RSPB Bempton Cliffs Visitor Centre
    • Spurn Discovery Centre, A Yorkshire Wildlife Trust visitor centre with an entry fee, the gateway to the reserve and home to the bird observatory's ringing station. It is the first stop for finding out what has been seen that morning.
  • Also covers: Beacon Ponds, Bridlington, Filey, Flamborough Cliffs Nature Reserve, Flamborough Head, South Landing, Kilnsea Wetlands Nature Reserve, Patrington, RSPB Bempton Cliffs Visitor Centre, Spurn Discovery Centre, Spurn National Nature Reserve, Spurn Point
  • Also watch for: Grey seals haul out on the sandbanks at the mouth of the Humber, visible from Spurn's point in good numbers through the winter. Harbour porpoises can be watched offshore from the Bempton clifftop through summer, and migrant moths and butterflies gather around Spurn's bushes each autumn.

The Wash and the Lincolnshire coast

Saltmarsh, mudflats and reedbed around the Wash and the Humber, on the open Lincolnshire coast

A vast square bay of sand and mud, with reserves along its southern and western edges and dune and saltmarsh running north. Wader and wildfowl counts here are among the highest anywhere in Britain.

  • Habitat: Vast intertidal sand and mud with saltmarsh, backed by reclaimed grazing and the dune ridge at Gibraltar Point.
  • When: October to March for the pink-footed geese and the wader roosts. Passage peaks in late summer with knot and godwit in five figures.
  • Getting there: Gibraltar Point is at the end of the road south from Skegness. Snettisham and Titchwell sit on the A149 round the Wash's eastern shore.
  • Look for: Red Knot, Bar-tailed Godwit, Pied Avocet, Common Shelduck, Western Marsh Harrier, Twite
  • Parks and reserves:
    • RSPB Frampton Marsh (RSPB reserve), An RSPB reserve on the edge of the Wash, free to enter and open every day. A visitor centre and screens look over freshwater scrapes holding avocets, knots and passage ruff.
    • RSPB Freiston Shore (RSPB reserve), An RSPB reserve of managed realignment saltmarsh on the Wash, walked freely along the seawall from a free car park. Shelduck, brent geese and huge wader roosts use it.
    • Gibraltar Point National Nature Reserve
    • Far Ings National Nature Reserve
    • RSPB Blacktoft Sands (RSPB reserve), An RSPB reserve holding the largest tidal reedbed on the Humber, with an entry fee for non-members. Six hides sit along a level path, and marsh harriers, bearded reedlings and passage waders use the reedbed.
  • Stops:
    • Gibraltar Point : A National Nature Reserve of dunes, saltmarsh and freshwater scrapes, with a visitor centre and free trails, open every day with no booking. Migrant passerines and wintering wildfowl come through.
    • Donna Nook : A National Nature Reserve on a military range, free and open outside range hours along a roped beach path. Grey seals pup in November and December, and shorebirds work the tideline.
    • Far Ings : A National Nature Reserve of old clay pits beside the Humber, free to enter every day. A visitor centre and hides are a short walk in, and bearded reedlings, bitterns and marsh harriers hold the reeds.
    • Alkborough Flats : A managed realignment wetland where the Trent, Ouse and Humber meet, free to visit with open access, a viewing platform and hides. Golden plover flock here and hen harriers hunt over the marsh.
    • Saltfleetby-Theddlethorpe Dunes : A National Nature Reserve of dunes and damp slacks on the open Lincolnshire coast, with free access along boardwalk trails and no booking. Migrant warblers pass through and twite flock in winter.
  • Visitor centres: RSPB Frampton Marsh Visitor Centre, Gibraltar Point Visitor Centre, Far Ings Visitor Centre
  • Also covers: Alkborough Flats, Barton-upon-Humber, Boston, Donna Nook, Far Ings National Nature Reserve, Far Ings Visitor Centre, Gibraltar Point National Nature Reserve, Gibraltar Point Visitor Centre, Grimsby, RSPB Blacktoft Sands, RSPB Frampton Marsh Visitor Centre, RSPB Freiston Shore, Saltfleetby-Theddlethorpe Dunes, Skegness
  • Also watch for: Grey seals gather to give birth on the beach at Donna Nook every November and December, with several thousand pups born along the roped viewing path. Brown hares box across the fields behind the sea banks in early spring, and water voles can be seen along the ditches at Far Ings and Frampton Marsh through the summer.

The Norfolk coast and the Broads

Norfolk's north coast and its inland reed country, two and a half hours from London by train

Shingle, saltmarsh and grazing marsh along the north coast, with reed fen and open water inland. More reserves sit within an hour of each other here than anywhere else in Britain, and the winter spectacle is on a European scale.

  • Habitat: Shingle ridge, dune, saltmarsh and grazing marsh along the north coast, with reedbed and grazing fen inland in the Broads.
  • When: Autumn is the reason people come, September to November for drift migrants and seawatching. Winter holds the geese and harriers, and May to July the terns and bitterns.
  • Getting there: The A149 runs the whole coast from Hunstanton to Cromer and every reserve is signed off it. The Coasthopper bus follows the same road, which is what makes a one-way walk possible.
  • Look for: Pied Avocet, Eurasian Bittern, Eurasian Spoonbill, Western Marsh Harrier, Common Crane, Bearded Reedling
  • Parks and reserves:
    • Broads National Park
    • Holkham National Nature Reserve, A National Nature Reserve of dune, pine woodland and saltmarsh, walked freely from several free car parks along the coast road. Pink-footed geese arrive in winter, spoonbills nest in the pines and a huge wader roost gathers on the flats.
    • Titchwell Marsh RSPB reserve
    • Cley Marshes, Norfolk Wildlife Trust (reserve)
    • Hickling Broad National Nature Reserve
  • Stops:
    • Titchwell Marsh : An RSPB reserve with a visitor centre and an entry fee for non-members. A level path and boardwalk run out to the beach, and one walk crosses three habitats holding avocet, marsh harrier and bearded reedling.
    • Cley Marshes : A Norfolk Wildlife Trust reserve with a visitor centre, hides and an entry fee, the oldest county Wildlife Trust reserve in Britain. Avocet and spoonbill work the scrapes, and bittern booms from the reedbed in spring.
    • Snettisham : An unstaffed RSPB reserve, free to enter from a roadside car park and a short walk along the sea wall. Tens of thousands of knot and other waders lift off the Wash on a rising tide.
    • Strumpshaw Fen : An RSPB reserve with a visitor centre and entry fee, on trails through reedbed, wet woodland and orchid meadow beside the River Yare. Marsh harrier and bittern hold the reeds, and a good day adds a swallowtail butterfly.
    • Hickling Broad : A Norfolk Wildlife Trust National Nature Reserve with a visitor centre, hides and a guided boat trip, entry fee for non-members. Marsh harrier and bittern hold the reeds, and it is the best chance in the Broads of common crane.
    • Horsey Windpump and Mere : A National Trust site with a windpump, car park and a network of free footpaths across the marshes. It is the centre of the reintroduced common crane population on the Norfolk Broads, with marsh harrier overhead.
    • The Yare valley at Buckenham and Cantley : Grazing marsh on the Yare with its own request-stop station. It holds the English taiga bean geese and a crane roost.
    • The Brecks : Sandy heath and pine belt inland of Thetford. Lynford Arboretum takes hawfinch and Santon Downham holds the woodland set.
  • Visitor centres: Cley Marshes Visitor Centre, Norfolk Wildlife Trust, Titchwell Marsh Visitor Centre, RSPB, Hickling Broad Visitor Centre, Norfolk Wildlife Trust
  • Also covers: Broads National Park, Cley Marshes Visitor Centre, Norfolk Wildlife Trust, Cley Marshes, Norfolk Wildlife Trust, Cley next the Sea, Hickling Broad National Nature Reserve, Hickling Broad Visitor Centre, Norfolk Wildlife Trust, Holkham National Nature Reserve, Holt, Horsey Windpump and Mere, Hunstanton, Ludham, Snettisham, Strumpshaw Fen, The Brecks, The Yare valley at Buckenham and Cantley, Titchwell Marsh RSPB reserve, Titchwell Marsh Visitor Centre, RSPB, Waxham and Horsey, Wells-next-the-Sea
  • Also watch for: Common and grey seals haul out at Blakeney Point all year and grey seal pups are born from October to January. Chinese water deer graze the Norfolk Broads reedbeds and marshes year round. Swallowtail butterflies live nowhere else in Britain and fly over the fens from late May to July.

Suffolk and the Essex coast

Reedbed, heath and shingle on a low estuary coast, two hours from London

Reedbed, heath and shingle running down to a low estuary coast. Minsmere is the reserve that made birdwatching popular in Britain, and the shingle at Orford Ness carries plants and birds found in very few other places.

  • Habitat: Reedbed, brackish scrape and shingle at Minsmere and Walberswick, with Sandlings heath behind and the Essex estuaries south of it.
  • When: April to July for bittern, marsh harrier, avocet and nightjar on the heaths. Winter fills the Essex estuaries with brent and waders.
  • Getting there: Minsmere is signed from the A12 through Westleton. Walberswick and Dunwich are reached on the same lanes, and Darsham is the nearest station.
  • Look for: Eurasian Bittern, Bearded Reedling, Pied Avocet, Western Marsh Harrier, Eurasian Spoonbill
  • Parks and reserves: RSPB Minsmere (RSPB reserve), Orford Ness National Nature Reserve
  • Stops:
    • Minsmere : An RSPB reserve with a visitor centre and an entry fee for non-members. Paths run through reedbed and heath to the beach, and bitterns, avocets and marsh harriers are here year round.
    • Dunwich Heath : A National Trust heathland reserve beside the beach, entered freely from its own car park. Dartford warblers, stonechats and nightjars hold the heather in summer.
    • Orford Ness : A shingle spit on a National Trust ferry booked in advance from Orford quay. Avocets, terns and rare shingle plants sit among former military buildings.
    • Abberton Reservoir : An Essex Wildlife Trust reserve with a visitor centre beside a working reservoir. Hides and a causeway give the views, and tens of thousands of wildfowl winter here.
    • Rainham Marshes : An RSPB reserve with a visitor centre on the Thames path east of London. Boardwalks cross the grazing marsh, and bearded reedlings, marsh harriers and water voles use it.
  • Visitor centres: RSPB Minsmere Visitor Centre, RSPB Rainham Marshes Visitor Centre
  • Also covers: Abberton Reservoir, Aldeburgh, Bradwell, Dunwich Heath, Maldon, Orford Ness National Nature Reserve, RSPB Minsmere Visitor Centre, RSPB Rainham Marshes Visitor Centre, Southwold, Westleton, Woodbridge
  • Also watch for: Adders and silver studded blue butterflies bask on the heather at Dunwich Heath and Dungeness through the summer months, and water voles search the ditches at Rainham Marshes from spring onward. Common seals haul out on the sandbanks of the Blackwater and Colne estuaries near Abberton, best watched as the tide falls.

The Chilterns, the Thames and the London reservoirs

Chalk escarpment, flooded gravel pit and reservoir on the edge of London

Chalk escarpment, gravel pit and working reservoir within reach of central London by train. Red kites released here in the eighties are now a common sight over the hills, and the wetlands hold bittern and marsh harrier. The Thames itself runs through the middle of it, and the reservoirs beside the river hold the wildfowl the region is worth a winter day for.

  • Habitat: Beech hangers and chalk downland over gravel-pit and reservoir country along the Thames and Lea valleys.
  • When: Year round. Red kite is resident and everywhere. The reservoirs take wildfowl and gulls from October, and passage terns and waders in spring.
  • Getting there: All of it is inside an hour of central London. The reservoirs at Staines and Walthamstow are on the Underground and Overground, and the Chiltern kites are visible from the M40.
  • Look for: Red Kite, Eurasian Hobby, Little Ringed Plover, Common Snipe, Western Marsh Harrier, Eurasian Bittern
  • Parks and reserves: Chilterns National Landscape, Lee Valley Regional Park (reserve), Colne Valley Regional Park (reserve)
  • Stops:
    • RSPB Otmoor : An RSPB reserve on reclaimed grazing marsh in Oxfordshire, open every day without charge along a bridleway from the car park. Marsh harrier, bittern and lapwing cross the reedbed.
    • College Lake : A Wildlife Trust reserve in a former chalk quarry near Tring, with a visitor centre and a small entry fee for non-members. Lapwing, snipe and little ringed plover use the pits.
    • The Chiltern red kites at Watlington Hill : A National Trust chalk hill in the Chilterns, open at any time with a free car park at Christmas Common. Red kites wheel overhead most days of the year.
    • WWT London Wetland Centre, Barnes : A WWT visitor centre and wetland reserve on former reservoirs at Barnes, with hides and an entry fee for non-members. Bittern, marsh harrier and wintering wildfowl use the lagoons.
    • : A working reservoir split into two basins by a causeway. The public footpath along the top gives the view, and rare gulls and wintering diving ducks gather on the water.
    • RSPB Rye Meads : An RSPB reserve with a visitor centre and boardwalk beside the River Lea, open every day with an entry fee for non-members. Kingfisher, common tern and bittern hold the reedbed.
    • Tring Reservoirs : Four canal feeder reservoirs on the Hertfordshire and Buckinghamshire border, on public paths from car parks at Wilstone and Marsworth. Hobbies hunt dragonflies over the water in summer.
  • Visitor centres: WWT London Wetland Centre, RSPB Rye Meads Visitor Centre, College Lake Visitor Centre (BBOWT)
  • Also covers: Chilterns National Landscape, College Lake Visitor Centre (BBOWT), Colne Valley Regional Park, Lee Valley Regional Park, Oxford, RSPB Otmoor, RSPB Rye Meads Visitor Centre, Staines Reservoir, The Chiltern red kites at Watlington Hill, Tring Reservoirs, Wallingford, Ware, WWT London Wetland Centre, Barnes
  • Also watch for: Fallow and muntjac deer move through the beechwoods of the Chilterns escarpment all year, and silver-spotted skippers and chalkhill blue butterflies fly over the flower-rich turf of Watlington Hill in July and August. Otters have returned to the rivers and lakes around Tring and Rye Meads after decades of absence, most often spotted at dawn or dusk.

Kent, Sussex and the south coast

Shingle spits, grazing marsh and chalk cliffs along the Channel

Shingle and chalk headland run along the Channel with grazing marsh behind, all within two hours of London. Dungeness is where a rarity can turn up in any month, and the Sheppey marshes hold wintering raptors in numbers.

  • Habitat: Shingle at Dungeness, chalk headland at Beachy Head and the grazing levels of Romney and Pevensey behind them.
  • When: Spring and autumn passage, when the headlands and the shingle concentrate whatever is moving. Dungeness seawatches best in an onshore spring wind.
  • Getting there: Dungeness is at the end of the road from Lydd. Beachy Head is above Eastbourne on the B2103, and Rye Harbour and Pett Level sit on the A259 between them.
  • Look for: Eurasian Bittern, Western Marsh Harrier, Bearded Reedling, Pied Avocet, Hen Harrier, Eurasian Hobby
  • Parks and reserves:
    • Dungeness National Nature Reserve
    • Elmley Nature Reserve, A privately run reserve on the Isle of Sheppey, entered along a mile-long farm track across grazing marsh for a small charge and no booking. Lapwings and redshanks hold the marsh and hen harriers hunt it.
    • Rye Harbour Nature Reserve, A National Nature Reserve of shingle and grazing marsh, open every day with a Discovery Centre and a network of free hides. Terns and avocets breed here and wildfowl winter on the pits.
    • Pagham Harbour Local Nature Reserve
    • RSPB Pulborough Brooks (RSPB reserve), An RSPB reserve on the Arun floodplain, with a visitor centre, cafe and trails through wet grassland, entry fee for non-members. Lapwings and wigeon winter here and hobbies hunt over it in summer.
  • Stops:
    • RSPB Dungeness : An RSPB reserve on Denge Beach's shingle, free to enter with paid parking. A visitor centre and hides ring the old gravel pits, and bitterns, marsh harriers and hobbies hold them.
    • Dungeness Bird Observatory : A working bird observatory beside the lighthouses, open to visitors with no need to book. Ringing demonstrations and the daily sightings log run through the season, and migrant thrushes, chats and falls of warblers arrive on the right wind.
    • Oare Marshes : A Kent Wildlife Trust reserve on the Swale, a short free circuit of scrapes and a sea wall from a small car park. Avocets, black-tailed godwits and passage waders use it.
    • : A local nature reserve around a tidal harbour, on the seawall path from car parks at Church Norton and Sidlesham Ferry. Brent geese, bar-tailed godwits and wintering waders work the mud.
    • Beachy Head : A chalk headland on open access land above England's highest chalk cliffs, free to walk with no booking. Peregrines and ravens hold the cliffs and passage migrants follow the edge.
  • Visitor centres: RSPB Dungeness Visitor Centre, RSPB Pulborough Brooks Visitor Centre
  • Also covers: Allhallows, Amberley Wild Brooks, Arundel, Beachy Head, Capel Fleet and Harty Ferry, Chichester, Chidham, Climping, Dungeness Bird Observatory, Dungeness National Nature Reserve, East Head and Snowhill Marsh, Eastbourne, Elmley Marshes, Elmley Nature Reserve, Farlington Marshes, Faversham, Fishbourne Channel, Fordwich, Funton Creek and Chetney, Grove Ferry, Halstow Marshes, Ham Green and Lower Halstow, Lade Sands and Lade Pit, Northward Hill, Oare Marshes, Pagham Harbour Local Nature Reserve, Riverside Country Park, RSPB Dungeness Visitor Centre, RSPB Pulborough Brooks Visitor Centre, Rye Harbour Nature Reserve, Scotney Pit and Walland Marsh, Selsey Bill, Shell Ness (Swale NNR), Stodmarsh, Thorney Island, Westbere Marshes
  • Also watch for: Common and grey seals haul out on the shingle at Rye Harbour and can often be seen offshore from Dungeness through the year. Adders and common lizards warm themselves on the shingle banks from March, and Dungeness holds one of the richest populations of moths and beetles found anywhere in Britain.

The Somerset Levels and the Severn

Restored peat wetland reedbeds and the tidal Severn, roughly two hours from London by train to Castle Cary or Bridgwater

Restored peat wetland below the Mendips and a vast tidal estuary west of it. The Levels now hold bitterns and a winter starling murmuration that draws crowds, and the Severn takes wild swans and geese from the Arctic.

  • Habitat: Peat moor turned to reedbed and open water in the Avalon Marshes, with the Severn's mud and saltmarsh at Slimbridge to the north.
  • When: November to February for the starling roosts and the Slimbridge swans and geese. April to July for bittern, crane and great egret on the Levels.
  • Getting there: The Avalon Marshes are signed off the A39 between Glastonbury and Wedmore. Slimbridge is two minutes from junction 13 of the M5.
  • Look for: Eurasian Bittern, Great Egret, Eurasian Hobby, Common Crane, Tundra Swan, Eurasian Spoonbill, Hawfinch
  • Parks and reserves:
    • Shapwick Heath National Nature Reserve, A National Nature Reserve on former peat workings, walked freely from the Sweet Track car park. Bitterns, great white egrets and otters work the ditches.
    • Westhay Moor Site of Special Scientific Interest (reserve)
    • Bridgwater Bay National Nature Reserve
    • Severn Estuary Site of Special Scientific Interest (reserve)
  • Stops:
    • RSPB Ham Wall : An RSPB reedbed reserve with free access from a roadside car park near Ashcott. Bitterns boom, hobbies hunt over the reeds, and huge starling murmurations gather in winter.
    • Westhay Moor : A Somerset Wildlife Trust reserve on flooded peat diggings, with a paid car park off the Westhay road. Bitterns and otters hold the water and a vast starling roost gathers in winter.
    • Catcott Complex : A Somerset Wildlife Trust reserve of flooded fields and reedbed, walked freely from a car park on Lady's Drove. Wigeon and teal winter here, and egrets and otters show from the Tower Hide.
    • WWT Steart Marshes : A WWT working wetland of saltmarsh and freshwater pools, open free of charge on paths from the visitor car park. Avocets and spoonbills breed and wildfowl winter on the Severn shore.
    • WWT Slimbridge : A WWT wetland centre with an entry fee, hides and heated lookouts over managed pools and the Severn saltings. It is the best place in England for wintering Bewick's swans.
    • : An open sea wall from a roadside parking spot near the old ferry crossing at New Passage. Wading birds and wildfowl work the tide across the Severn.
    • RSPB Swell Wood : An RSPB woodland reserve with a car park and hide overlooking the closed West Sedgemoor marsh. Herons breed in the wood and reintroduced common cranes arrive in winter.
    • The Forest of Dean : Ancient oak and beech above the Wye, and the most reliable Hawfinch and Goshawk ground in England. The Nagshead and Cannop car parks are where to start.
    • Shapwick Heath : A national nature reserve managed by Natural England, on boardwalks from two car parks beside Ham Wall. Bitterns, hobbies and otters work the old peat workings.
  • Visitor centres: Avalon Marshes Centre, WWT Slimbridge Wetland Centre, WWT Steart Marshes Visitor Centre
  • Also covers: Avalon Marshes Centre, Bridgwater Bay National Nature Reserve, Catcott Complex, Frampton, Glastonbury, RSPB Ham Wall, RSPB Swell Wood, Severn Estuary Site of Special Scientific Interest, Shapwick Heath National Nature Reserve, The Forest of Dean, The Severn Estuary at New Passage, Wedmore, Westhay Moor Site of Special Scientific Interest, WWT Slimbridge Wetland Centre, WWT Steart Marshes Visitor Centre
  • Also watch for: Otters and water voles work the drainage rhynes and are most reliably seen at dawn, while roe deer graze the willow carr year round. Adders bask on the drier tracks of Shapwick Heath in March and April, and dragonflies including the hairy dragonfly and four-spotted chaser fill the reedbeds from May to August.

The New Forest, Dorset and Poole Harbour

Heathland, harbour and chalk coast around Bournemouth and Weymouth, under two hours from London by train to Poole or Weymouth

Ancient wood pasture and open heath running down to a shallow harbour and a chalk headland. The heaths carry Dartford warblers and nightjars, and Portland Bill logs whatever is passing offshore.

  • Habitat: Lowland heath and ancient pasture woodland, with harbour mudflat, reedbed and the Purbeck cliffs to the south.
  • When: May to July for nightjar, woodlark and Dartford warbler on the heath. Winter fills Poole Harbour with avocet, black-tailed godwit and grebes.
  • Getting there: The A31 and A35 cross the Forest, and Brockenhurst and Beaulieu Road have stations on the line through it. Arne is signed off the A351 south of Wareham.
  • Look for: Dartford Warbler, European Nightjar, Osprey, Eurasian Spoonbill, Sandwich Tern, Pied Avocet
  • Parks and reserves: New Forest National Park, Poole Harbour Site of Special Scientific Interest (reserve), Durlston National Nature Reserve, Dorset and East Devon Coast World Heritage Site (reserve)
  • Stops:
    • Acres Down : An open heath in the New Forest, walked freely from a Forestry England car park at Acres Down. It is one of England's few reliable spots for honey buzzard and hobby overhead.
    • RSPB Arne : An RSPB heathland reserve with a visitor centre, cafe and an entry fee, on the shore of Poole Harbour. Dartford warblers, nightjars and spoonbills hold it, and reintroduced ospreys pass overhead.
    • Brownsea Island : A Dorset Wildlife Trust island in Poole Harbour, by ferry from Poole Quay with an entry fee. Terns and avocets use the lagoon and red squirrels hold the woods.
    • : A working headland with a bird observatory in the old lower lighthouse, staffed by volunteer ringers. It is the top seabird watchpoint on the Dorset coast for shearwaters and skuas.
    • RSPB Radipole Lake : An RSPB reedbed reserve in central Weymouth, with a discovery centre and free access from the bus and rail stations. Bearded tits, bitterns and marsh harriers hold the reeds beside the shops.
    • RSPB Lodmoor : An RSPB wetland reserve on the edge of Weymouth, with free access from a seafront car park. Bearded tits and Cetti's warblers hold the reeds and migrant waders drop in on passage.
    • Durlston Country Park : A Dorset Council country park and National Nature Reserve on the Purbeck cliffs, with a castle visitor centre and free access. Guillemots and razorbills breed below and seabirds pass offshore.
    • : A headland and local nature reserve at the mouth of Christchurch Harbour, walked freely from a large car park. It is a well watched migration point for warblers and passing seabirds.
    • Keyhaven and Pennington Marshes : Lagoon, saltmarsh and shingle on the Solent behind Hurst Spit. The sea wall from Keyhaven quay is the walk.
    • : A roadside car park and open heath in the New Forest, walked freely with no facilities on site. Honey buzzards and goshawks display overhead in early spring, and woodlarks and hobbies hold it in summer.
    • Portland Bill : A bird observatory on the southern tip of Portland, open to all from the coast path and the observatory garden. Migrant passerines and seabird passage fill spring and autumn.
  • Visitor centres: RSPB Arne visitor centre, Durlston Castle, Wild Weymouth Discovery Centre, Radipole Lake
  • Also covers: Acres Down, the New Forest, Ashley Walk and Hampton Ridge, Beaulieu Road, Blashford Lakes Wildlife Reserve, Bolderwood, Brockenhurst, Brownsea Island, Christchurch Harbour, Dorset and East Devon Coast World Heritage Site, Durlston Castle, Durlston Country Park, Durlston Head, Durlston National Nature Reserve, Eyeworth Pond and Fritham, Hengistbury Head, Keyhaven and Pennington Marshes, Lymington, New Forest National Park, Poole Harbour Site of Special Scientific Interest, Portland Bill and the Bird Observatory, RSPB Arne visitor centre, RSPB Lodmoor, RSPB Radipole Lake, Stanpit Marsh, Studland Heath, Wareham, Wild Weymouth Discovery Centre, Radipole Lake
  • Also watch for: Sika deer roam the heath and reedbeds around Poole Harbour and are most vocal during their rut in October, while Brownsea Island holds one of southern England's few surviving red squirrel populations. Adders and sand lizards bask on the Dorset heaths in spring, and grey seals haul out on the ledges below Durlston through the year.

Cornwall, Devon and the Isles of Scilly

Granite headlands, tidal estuaries and an offshore archipelago, from Penzance out to islands reached by ferry or plane

A long granite peninsula ending in an Atlantic archipelago twenty eight miles past Land's End. Scilly is where Britain's rarities arrive each October, and the south Devon estuaries hold cirl buntings and wintering waders.

  • Habitat: Granite headland and sheltered estuary on the mainland, with the low granite islands and bulb fields of Scilly offshore.
  • When: October is Scilly's month and the reason the archipelago has its reputation. Seawatching off the mainland headlands runs July to October in a westerly.
  • Getting there: Scilly is reached by the Penzance ferry or the Land's End and Newquay flights, and October bookings go early. The mainland headlands are all within an hour of Penzance.
  • Look for: Manx Shearwater, European Storm Petrel, Sooty Shearwater, Red-billed Chough, Cirl Bunting, Eurasian Spoonbill
  • Parks and reserves: Isles of Scilly Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty (National Landscape), Cornwall National Landscape, West Penwith, Lundy Marine Conservation Zone (reserve), Exe Estuary Site of Special Scientific Interest (reserve)
  • Stops:
    • RSPB Marazion Marsh : An RSPB reedbed reserve behind Marazion beach, walked freely from nearby pay and display parking. Cornwall's largest reedbed holds bitterns, and huge starling murmurations gather over Mount's Bay in autumn.
    • RSPB Hayle Estuary : An RSPB estuary reserve at Ryan's Field off Chenhalls Road in Hayle, open at all times. Up to eighteen thousand ducks and waders work the mud in winter.
    • Porthgwarra : A fishing cove below the coast path near Land's End, free to walk from a National Trust car park. It is Cornwall's classic autumn watchpoint for rare migrants and passing seabirds.
    • Land's End : A National Trust headland and England's most westerly point, with open clifftop paths and no fee to walk them. Choughs hold the cliffs and it is a fine seabird watchpoint for shearwaters.
    • Isles of Scilly : An archipelago of five inhabited islands, by ferry from Penzance or plane from Land's End, walked freely on open paths. It is Britain's foremost autumn magnet for rare migrant birds.
    • RSPB Exminster and Powderham Marshes : An RSPB wetland reserve beside the Exe estuary, with free access and a car park off the old Exeter canal path. Brent geese and wigeon winter here and peregrines hunt the flats.
    • RSPB Bowling Green Marsh : An RSPB hide and viewing platform on the Exe estuary at Topsham, free to visit at any time. Avocets and godwits work the mud, and some winters bring a spoonbill.
    • Lundy : A granite island in the Bristol Channel, on the MS Oldenburg from Bideford or Ilfracombe, with a landing fee on arrival. It holds England's largest Manx shearwater colony and breeding puffins.
  • Visitor centres: Isles of Scilly Wildlife Trust, Cornwall Wildlife Trust, RSPB Exe Estuary reserves office, Darts Farm
  • Also covers: Bideford, Cornwall National Landscape, West Penwith, Cornwall Wildlife Trust, Dawlish Warren, Exe Estuary Site of Special Scientific Interest, Exeter, Exminster Marshes, Exmouth, Hugh Town, Isles of Scilly Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, Isles of Scilly Wildlife Trust, Land's End, Lundy Marine Conservation Zone, Penzance, Porthgwarra, RSPB Bowling Green Marsh, RSPB Exe Estuary reserves office, Darts Farm, RSPB Exminster and Powderham Marshes, RSPB Hayle Estuary, RSPB Marazion Marsh, Sennen Cove, St Just
  • Also watch for: Grey seals haul out on rocks around the Isles of Scilly and Godrevy year round and pup on the quieter beaches from August to November. Atlantic common dolphins and harbour porpoises show regularly from the Porthgwarra and Land's End coast path. Basking sharks pass close inshore off west Cornwall from May to July and feed at the surface on the summer plankton blooms.

Preparation

BeakBrain Learn the English list before you travel Collector cards for every species above, with short daily rounds that teach them by sight and sound. Learn these 681 birds before you fly

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the best time to go birding in England?

May and June for seabird colonies, heathland and full song together. September and October for passage on both coasts, and October on Scilly for American vagrants. December to February for waders and wildfowl on the estuaries, which is when the biggest counts happen.

Where should I go for a first English birding trip?

North Norfolk. Cley, Titchwell, Holkham and Snettisham sit along twenty-five miles of one coast road, and between them they cover reedbed, saltmarsh, freshwater scrape and tidal flat. It works in every month of the year and there is more written about it than anywhere else in England.

Do I need a car?

Less than in most countries. Rainham, Dungeness, Bempton, Leighton Moss and Slimbridge are all reachable by train and a short walk or taxi, and the Coasthopper bus runs the whole north Norfolk coast road. A car still helps in the New Forest, the Peak District and the Somerset Levels, where reserves are spread out and buses are thin.

Which English birds are hard to find elsewhere in Britain?

Dartford Warbler, Nightingale, Turtle Dove, Stone-curlew, Cirl Bunting and Bittern are all far more findable in England than in Scotland or Wales, and most of them are effectively confined to the south. Cirl Bunting in particular is down to south Devon and a small reintroduced Cornish population.

Is Scilly worth it in October?

If you want the chance of an American passerine, yes, and nowhere else in Britain compares. It is a long journey and the weather decides everything, so go for the islands and treat the rarities as the bonus rather than the plan.

What is the best wader spectacle in England?

Snettisham on the Wash, on a spring tide of about 8 metres. The rising water pushes tens of thousands of knot and godwit off the mud and onto the pits behind the shingle, and the flocks move as one. Check the tide tables before you commit to a date.

Can I see Red Kite easily?

Yes. The Chilterns reintroduction has been so successful that kites are now a normal roadside bird along the M40 and across much of central southern England. No reserve is needed.

How much does an English birding trip cost?

Accommodation is the largest line and varies enormously by season and region. Almost every reserve above is free to walk or costs a small entry, and RSPB or Wildlife Trust membership covers most of the charged ones.

Do I need to book the island boats?

For the Farne Islands in June and July, yes, well ahead. Scilly flights and the Scillonian also fill in October. Bempton, Spurn and the mainland reserves need no booking at all.

Can I bird here with limited mobility?

Often yes, and it varies by site. A good deal of the birding here happens from roadsides, hides and lodge grounds rather than on long walks, and some reserves keep flat, surfaced trails. Ask a lodge or reserve directly about step free access, surfaces and seating before you book. The Birdability Map records those details for birding sites, and their Access Considerations guide lists the questions worth asking. Coverage is thin outside the United States, so read a blank area as unrecorded rather than unsuitable.

Birding Community

Alongside the national bodies below, England has 43 local bird clubs across 42 regions. See every English club by region.

RSPB BirdLife in the UK, and the owner of a great many of the reserves above. Membership pays for itself quickly if you plan to visit more than a handful. Visit BTO The British Trust for Ornithology, which runs the national surveys and ringing scheme, and publishes the population figures for every British breeding bird. Visit The Wildlife Trusts Forty-six county trusts own many of the smaller reserves named here. Spurn and much of the Somerset Levels are among them. Visit WWT The Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust, which runs Slimbridge on the Severn and several other wetland centres. Visit BirdGuides The national sightings and rarity service, and how English birders find out what has turned up where. Visit
